Reference: Ahlfeldt et al. (2015)

Model Setting

The paper asks how strong agglomeration and dispersion forces are inside a city, and how they can be separated from variation in locational fundamentals. High land prices and dense activity in a group of neighboring blocks are consistent with strong agglomeration forces, but also with shared natural advantages (access to water) or shared amenities (leafy streets). The paper makes two contributions. First, it develops a quantitative model of internal city structure with an arbitrary number of heterogeneous blocks, endogenous commuting, endogenous land use, production externalities and residential externalities, which remains tractable because workers draw idiosyncratic Frechet shocks over pairs of residence and workplace. Second, it combines the model with the division and reunification of Berlin as an exogenous source of variation in the surrounding concentration of economic activity, using newly collected data on land prices, workplace employment and residence employment for 15,937 blocks in 1936, 1986 and 2006.

The empirical analysis has three layers. Reduced-form difference-in-differences regressions show that division reoriented the gradient of floor prices and employment in West Berlin away from the pre-war central business district (CBD), which lay just east of the Wall, and that reunification brought this gradient back. A commuting gravity equation delivers the commuting parameters and, through the recursive structure of the model, overall productivity and amenities for every block; a version of the model in which these are exogenous cannot reproduce the reduced-form effects. A generalized method of moments (GMM) estimation that uses division and reunification then identifies the agglomeration parameters. The central estimates are an elasticity of productivity with respect to the surrounding density of workplace employment of 0.07 and an elasticity of amenities with respect to the surrounding density of residents of 0.15; both externalities are highly localized and fall to nearly zero after about ten minutes of travel time. With these estimates the model accounts for the observed effects of division and reunification.

Environment and Preferences

A city is embedded in a wider economy and consists of discrete blocks i=1,…,Si=1,\ldots,Si=1,…,S. It is populated by an endogenous measure HHH of workers who are perfectly mobile within the city and the wider economy, where they can obtain the reservation utility Uˉ\bar{U}Uˉ. Each block has a supply of floor space LiL_iLi​, of which a share θi\theta_iθi​ is used commercially and 1−θi1-\theta_i1−θi​ residentially. Firms produce a single final good that is traded costlessly inside the city and with the wider economy and serves as the numeraire. A worker decides whether to move to the city before observing her idiosyncratic shocks; if she moves, she observes one shock for every pair of residence block and workplace block and picks the pair that maximizes utility. Blocks differ in final goods productivity AiA_iAi​, residential amenities BiB_iBi​, floor space and access to the transport network, summarized by bilateral travel times τij\tau_{ij}τij​ in minutes.

Workers are risk neutral. Worker ooo living in block iii and working in block jjj has utility equal to a Cobb-Douglas consumption index:

A higher wage in jjj or better amenities in iii raise the utility of a worker with a given draw, but they also attract workers with lower draws; under the Frechet distribution the two effects offset exactly. Attractive pairs therefore absorb more commuters on the extensive margin until expected utility is equalized across pairs, and average utility does not vary with the length of the commute.

Commuting Market Clearing and Expected Income

Commuting market clearing requires that the measure of workers employed in block jjj equals the measure of residents of all blocks who choose to commute to jjj:

HMj=∑i=1SEj(wj/dij)ε∑s=1SEs(ws/dis)εHRi(17)H_{Mj}=\sum_{i=1}^{S}\frac{E_j(w_j/d_{ij})^{\varepsilon}}{\sum_{s=1}^{S}E_s(w_s/d_{is})^{\varepsilon}}H_{Ri} \tag{17}HMj​=i=1∑S​∑s=1S​Es​(ws​/dis​)εEj​(wj​/dij​)ε​HRi​(17)

Since there is a continuum of workers in every block, there is no uncertainty in labor supply, and the supply of commuters to each workplace is a continuously increasing function of its wage relative to other wages. Without preference heterogeneity, small wage changes would move all residents of a block from one workplace to another, which is implausible and makes the equilibrium with asymmetric locations hard to determine. Expected worker income conditional on living in block iii weights wages by the conditional commuting probabilities:

E[wj∣i]=∑j=1SEj(wj/dij)ε∑s=1SEs(ws/dis)εwj(18)\mathbb{E}[w_j\mid i]=\sum_{j=1}^{S}\frac{E_j(w_j/d_{ij})^{\varepsilon}}{\sum_{s=1}^{S}E_s(w_s/d_{is})^{\varepsilon}}w_j \tag{18}E[wj​∣i]=j=1∑S​∑s=1S​Es​(ws​/dis​)εEj​(wj​/dij​)ε​wj​(18)

Expected income is high in blocks with low commuting costs to high-wage workplaces.

General Equilibrium with Exogenous Location Characteristics

Given the parameters {α,β,μ,ε,κ}\{\alpha,\beta,\mu,\varepsilon,\kappa\}{α,β,μ,ε,κ}, the reservation utility Uˉ\bar{U}Uˉ and exogenous location characteristics {T,E,A,B,φ,K,ξ,τ}\{\mathbf{T},\mathbf{E},\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B},\boldsymbol{\varphi},\mathbf{K},\boldsymbol{\xi},\boldsymbol{\tau}\}{T,E,A,B,φ,K,ξ,τ}, a general equilibrium is a vector {πM,πR,H,Q,q,w,θ}\{\boldsymbol{\pi}_M,\boldsymbol{\pi}_R,H,\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{q},\mathbf{w},\boldsymbol{\theta}\}{πM​,πR​,H,Q,q,w,θ} that satisfies seven sets of conditions: population mobility, the residential choice probabilities, the workplace choice probabilities, commercial land market clearing, residential land market clearing, zero profits, and no-arbitrage between land uses.

Proposition 1. If TiT_iTi​, EiE_iEi​, φi\varphi_iφi​, KiK_iKi​, ξi\xi_iξi​ and τij\tau_{ij}τij​ are exogenous, finite and strictly positive, and Ai∈[0,∞)A_i\in[0,\infty)Ai​∈[0,∞) and Bi∈[0,∞)B_i\in[0,\infty)Bi​∈[0,∞) are exogenous, finite and nonnegative, there exists a unique general equilibrium vector.

The appendix proves this in steps. Because the support of the Frechet distribution is unbounded from above, every block with a strictly positive and finite wage attracts a positive measure of workers, and every block with a strictly positive and finite floor price attracts a positive measure of residents (Lemma S.1). The appendix extends the result to blocks without workers or residents. Agglomeration Forces

Productivity depends on production fundamentals aja_jaj​ (features of physical geography such as access to natural water) and production externalities Υj\Upsilon_jΥj​, which are a travel-time weighted sum of workplace employment density in surrounding blocks:

Aj=ajΥjλ,Υj≡∑s=1Se−δτjs(HMsKs)(30)A_j=a_j\Upsilon_j^{\lambda},\qquad \Upsilon_j\equiv\sum_{s=1}^{S}e^{-\delta\tau_{js}}\left(\frac{H_{Ms}}{K_s}\right) \tag{30}Aj​=aj​Υjλ​,Υj​≡s=1∑S​e−δτjs​(Ks​HMs​​)(30)

where δ\deltaδ is the rate of spatial decay and λ\lambdaλ the elasticity of productivity with respect to the surrounding density of employment. Density is measured per unit of land area rather than floor space, so that higher ratios of floor space to land raise the surrounding concentration of activity. The canonical interpretation is knowledge spillovers. Amenities are modeled symmetrically, as the product of residential fundamentals bib_ibi​ (such as green areas) and residential externalities Ωi\Omega_iΩi​:

Bi=biΩiη,Ωi≡∑r=1Se−ρτir(HRrKr)(31)B_i=b_i\Omega_i^{\eta},\qquad \Omega_i\equiv\sum_{r=1}^{S}e^{-\rho\tau_{ir}}\left(\frac{H_{Rr}}{K_r}\right) \tag{31}Bi​=bi​Ωiη​,Ωi​≡r=1∑S​e−ρτir​(Kr​HRr​​)(31)

where ρ\rhoρ is the rate of spatial decay and η\etaη captures the net effect of the surrounding density of residents on amenities, including negative spillovers (air pollution, crime) and positive ones (urban amenities). η\etaη is only the direct effect on utility; general equilibrium effects through floor prices, commuting and wages come on top.

With finite decay rates, Υj\Upsilon_jΥj​ and Ωi\Omega_iΩi​ are strictly positive in every block as long as there is employment somewhere, so the lemmas above carry over with aia_iai​ and bib_ibi​ replacing AiA_iAi​ and BiB_iBi​: blocks with positive fundamentals are incompletely specialized, and zero workplace (residence) employment requires ai=0a_i=0ai​=0 (bi=0b_i=0bi​=0) (Lemmas S.4 and S.5). Uniqueness does not carry over. Each agent's location decision depends on productivity and amenities, which in turn depend on the location decisions of all agents, so the model may have multiple equilibria if the agglomeration forces, governed by {λ,η}\{\lambda,\eta\}{λ,η} and {δ,ρ}\{\delta,\rho\}{δ,ρ}, are strong relative to the exogenous differences across locations. The paper does not derive a condition for uniqueness in this case; instead, the empirical approach is built so that it is valid whether or not the equilibrium is unique.

Proposition 2. (i) Given the parameters {α,β,μ,ε,κ}\{\alpha,\beta,\mu,\varepsilon,\kappa\}{α,β,μ,ε,κ} and the observed data {Q,HM,HR,K,τ}\{\mathbb{Q},\mathbf{H}_M,\mathbf{H}_R,\mathbf{K},\boldsymbol{\tau}\}{Q,HM​,HR​,K,τ}, there exist unique vectors {A~∗,B~∗,φ~∗}\{\tilde{\mathbf{A}}^{*},\tilde{\mathbf{B}}^{*},\tilde{\boldsymbol{\varphi}}^{*}\}{A~∗,B~∗,φ~​∗} consistent with the data being an equilibrium of the model. The key point is that in a model with multiple equilibria the mapping from fundamentals to endogenous variables is not unique, but the inverse mapping from observed endogenous variables to fundamentals can still be unique. Here it is, because the equilibrium conditions (profit maximization, zero profits, utility maximization, population mobility, market clearing) hold in any equilibrium, since agents are atomistic and take the behavior of others as given. The result needs all five observed variables; without any one of them the fundamentals would be under-identified. The proof is recursive and constructive.

Division and Reunification in the Model

In 1936 Berlin was approximately monocentric, with the highest land values in the CBD in the district Mitte, which became part of East Berlin; the Kudamm in the later West Berlin was a secondary center. The city was divided into occupation sectors along the 1938 district boundaries, a choice driven by military considerations. The border inside Berlin stayed formally open, with some commuting across it, until the construction of the Wall in 1961 ended all local economic interactions between East and West Berlin; the Wall fell in 1989, Germany was formally reunified in 1990, and rail lines and utility networks were rapidly reconnected. The analysis focuses on West Berlin, which remained a market economy. Division is modeled as infinite costs of trading the final good, infinite commuting costs (κ→∞\kappa\to\inftyκ→∞) and infinite decay of production and residential externalities (δ→∞\delta\to\inftyδ→∞, ρ→∞\rho\to\inftyρ→∞) across the Wall. West Berlin blocks lose (1) employment opportunities in East Berlin, (2) commuters from East Berlin, (3) production externalities from East Berlin, and (4) residential externalities from East Berlin. All four effects reduce expected utility, so population falls, and all four are stronger close to the pre-war concentrations of employment and residents in East Berlin, so floor prices, workplace employment and residence employment should fall there relative to the rest of West Berlin. Reunification should have the opposite effects, though not necessarily of the same size: with multiple equilibria division could have shifted the city to a different equilibrium, and East Berlin itself changed between 1936 and 2006.

Data and Reduced-Form Evidence

The data cover 15,937 statistical blocks (just under 9,000 in the former West Berlin), with a mean area of about 50,000 square meters, for all of Berlin in 1936 and 2006 and for West Berlin in 1986. Workplace employment comes from the 1933 census combined with the 1931 company register, the 1987 census and 2003 social security records; residence employment from the 1933 and 1987 censuses and 2005 population registers; land values from Kalweit (1937) and the Committee of Valuation Experts (1986, 2006), converted to floor prices with the construction technology; and travel times from minimum travel time calculations on the public transport network of each year (underground, suburban rail, tram, bus and walking), combined in 1986 and 2006 with driving times weighted by modal shares. Additional data are commuting surveys for 1936, 1982 and 2008 and wages by workplace district for West Berlin in 1986.

The reduced-form specification, estimated separately for division (1936 to 1986) and reunification (1986 to 2006), is:

Δln⁡Oi=α+∑k=1KIikβk+ln⁡Miγ+ui(41)\Delta\ln O_i=\alpha+\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathbb{I}_{ik}\beta_k+\ln M_i\gamma+u_i \tag{41}ΔlnOi​=α+k=1∑K​Iik​βk​+lnMi​γ+ui​(41)

where Δln⁡Oi\Delta\ln O_iΔlnOi​ is the log change in floor prices, workplace employment or residence employment of block iii, Iik\mathbb{I}_{ik}Iik​ indicates that block iii lies in distance grid cell kkk from the pre-war CBD (six cells of 500 meters; the excluded category is blocks more than 3.75 kilometers away), MiM_iMi​ are time-invariant block characteristics whose premium may change over time, and uiu_iui​ is an error; in this equation only, α\alphaα, βk\beta_kβk​ and γ\gammaγ denote regression coefficients. Standard errors allow for spatial correlation within 0.5 kilometers following Conley (1999).

  • Division: floor prices in the first grid cell fall by 0.800 log points (55 percent) relative to blocks beyond 3.75 kilometers, and the effect declines monotonically with distance (−0.291-0.291−0.291 in the sixth cell); the six cells alone explain a quarter of the variation. With district fixed effects, grid cells for distance to the inner and outer boundaries and to the Kudamm, and block controls, the first-cell coefficient is −0.565-0.565−0.565. Residence employment falls by 1.332 and workplace employment by 0.691 log points in the first cell.

  • Reunification: floor prices in the first cell rise by 0.398 log points (49 percent), residence employment by 1.079 and workplace employment by 1.574 log points; the effects are smaller, more localized and less precisely estimated than for division.

  • Coefficients on distance to other segments of the Wall are close to zero, so the mechanism is the loss of access to the pre-war CBD and not proximity to the Wall as such. Most of the division effect had occurred by 1966, and there are no pre-trends in 1928 to 1936 or 1966 to 1986. The population of West Berlin fell from 2.68 million in 1933 to 2.01 million in 1987.

Gravity, Calibration and the Model without Externalities

Taking logs of the bilateral commuting probability gives a semi-log gravity equation, in which the denominator Φ\PhiΦ is absorbed by the fixed effects:

ln⁡πij=−ντij+ϑi+ςj+eij(42)\ln\pi_{ij}=-\nu\tau_{ij}+\vartheta_i+\varsigma_j+e_{ij} \tag{42}lnπij​=−ντij​+ϑi​+ςj​+eij​(42)

where ϑi\vartheta_iϑi​ are residence fixed effects (capturing {Bi,Ti,Qi}\{B_i,T_i,Q_i\}{Bi​,Ti​,Qi​}), ςj\varsigma_jςj​ are workplace fixed effects (capturing {wj,Ej}\{w_j,E_j\}{wj​,Ej​}), ν=εκ\nu=\varepsilon\kappaν=εκ is the semi-elasticity of commuting flows with respect to travel time, and eije_{ij}eij​ is measurement error in travel times. The equation is estimated on a 2008 survey of 7,948 commuters aggregated to the 144 pairs of the 12 districts, averaging within district pairs. The estimate is ν^=0.0697\hat{\nu}=0.0697ν^=0.0697 by ordinary least squares, 0.0702 for pairs with at least 10 commuters (with an R2R^2R2 of 0.91), 0.0771 by Poisson and 0.0706 by Gamma pseudo maximum likelihood: each additional minute of travel time reduces commuting flows by about 7 percent. With ν=0.07\nu=0.07ν=0.07 the system in transformed wages is solved for every year, which yields commuting flows between all blocks. As a check on moments not used in estimation, the model reproduces the cumulative distribution of commuters across travel time bins in 2008, in West Berlin in 1982 and in Berlin in 1936.

Three parameters are set from the literature: the share of residential floor space in consumer expenditure 1−β=0.251-\beta=0.251−β=0.25 (Davis and Ortalo-Magne 2011), the share of commercial floor space in firm costs 1−α=0.201-\alpha=0.201−α=0.20 (Valentinyi and Herrendorf 2008) and the share of land in construction costs 1−μ=0.251-\mu=0.251−μ=0.25 (Combes, Duranton and Gobillon 2014; Epple, Gordon and Sieg 2010), the last also supported by micro data on property transactions in Berlin. Since σln⁡w~it2=(1/ε)2σln⁡ωit2\sigma^2_{\ln\tilde{w}_{it}}=(1/\varepsilon)^2\sigma^2_{\ln\omega_{it}}σlnw~it​2​=(1/ε)2σlnωit​2​, the Frechet shape parameter is chosen to match the variance of log wages across West Berlin districts in 1986, which gives ε=6.83\varepsilon=6.83ε=6.83 and hence κ=ν/ε=0.01\kappa=\nu/\varepsilon=0.01κ=ν/ε=0.01. In logs and relative to geometric means (denoted by a bar), adjusted productivity and amenities are:

Using these recovered objects as dependent variables in the reduced-form specification, adjusted productivity in the first grid cell falls by 0.207 log points and adjusted amenities by 0.347 log points after division, and they rise by 0.261 and 0.203 after reunification. Productivity and amenities are therefore not invariant to the surrounding concentration of activity. Counterfactuals with exogenous location characteristics, which have determinate predictions by Proposition 1, confirm this: holding {A~i,B~i,φ~i}\{\tilde{A}_i,\tilde{B}_i,\tilde{\varphi}_i\}{A~i​,B~i​,φ~​i​} at their 1936 values, division lowers floor prices in the first cell by 0.408 log points, about half of the observed 0.800, with almost no gradient across the cells (between −0.35-0.35−0.35 and −0.41-0.41−0.41); holding West Berlin at its 1986 values, reunification changes them by −0.010-0.010−0.010 against an observed 0.398. Lost access to jobs and commuters alone cannot explain the data.

Structural Estimation: Residuals and Moment Conditions

The estimation recovers Λ={ν,ε,λ,δ,η,ρ}\Lambda=\{\nu,\varepsilon,\lambda,\delta,\eta,\rho\}Λ={ν,ε,λ,δ,η,ρ} jointly, keeping {α,β,μ}\{\alpha,\beta,\mu\}{α,β,μ} at the values above. Each fundamental is assumed to consist of a time-invariant block effect and a time-varying shock. Taking the change before and after division (or reunification), denoted by Δ\DeltaΔ, removes the block effect, and normalizing by the geometric mean in each year removes anything common to all blocks, such as Uˉt\bar{U}_tUˉt​ or the choice of units. The resulting double-differenced structural residuals are closed-form functions of data and parameters:

Δln⁡(a~ita~‾t)=(1−α)Δln⁡(QitQ‾t)+αεΔln⁡(ωitω‾t)−λΔln⁡(ΥitΥ‾t)(45)\Delta\ln\left(\frac{\tilde{a}_{it}}{\overline{\tilde{a}}_t}\right)=(1-\alpha)\Delta\ln\left(\frac{\mathbb{Q}_{it}}{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_t}\right)+\frac{\alpha}{\varepsilon}\Delta\ln\left(\frac{\omega_{it}}{\overline{\omega}_t}\right)-\lambda\Delta\ln\left(\frac{\Upsilon_{it}}{\overline{\Upsilon}_t}\right) \tag{45}Δln(a~t​a~it​​)=(1−α)Δln(Q​t​Qit​​)+εα​Δln(ωt​ωit​​)−λΔln(Υt​Υit​​)(45)
Δln⁡(b~itb~‾t)=1εΔln⁡(HRitH‾Rt)+(1−β)Δln⁡(QitQ‾t)−1εΔln⁡(WitW‾t)−ηΔln⁡(ΩitΩ‾t)(46)\Delta\ln\left(\frac{\tilde{b}_{it}}{\overline{\tilde{b}}_t}\right)=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\Delta\ln\left(\frac{H_{Rit}}{\overline{H}_{Rt}}\right)+(1-\beta)\Delta\ln\left(\frac{\mathbb{Q}_{it}}{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}_t}\right)-\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\Delta\ln\left(\frac{W_{it}}{\overline{W}_t}\right)-\eta\Delta\ln\left(\frac{\Omega_{it}}{\overline{\Omega}_t}\right) \tag{46}Δln(b~t​b~it​​)=ε1​Δln(HRt​HRit​​)+(1−β)Δln(Q​t​Qit​​)−ε1​Δln(Wt​Wit​​)−ηΔln(Ωt​Ωit​​)(46)

where Υit\Upsilon_{it}Υit​ and Ωit\Omega_{it}Ωit​ are computed from observed employment densities and travel times; in the estimation the own block is excluded from these sums to rule out a mechanical correlation. The identifying assumption is that these changes in fundamentals are uncorrelated with the change in the surrounding concentration of economic activity caused by division and reunification, which is captured by indicators Ik\mathbb{I}_kIk​, k∈{1,…,KI}k\in\{1,\ldots,K_{\mathbb{I}}\}k∈{1,…,KI​}, for 50 percentiles of distance to the pre-war CBD:

E[Ik×Δln⁡(a~it/a~‾t)]=0,E[Ik×Δln⁡(b~it/b~‾t)]=0,k∈{1,…,KI}(47)\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{I}_k\times\Delta\ln\left(\tilde{a}_{it}/\overline{\tilde{a}}_t\right)\right]=0,\qquad \mathbb{E}\left[\mathbb{I}_k\times\Delta\ln\left(\tilde{b}_{it}/\overline{\tilde{b}}_t\right)\right]=0,\qquad k\in\{1,\ldots,K_{\mathbb{I}}\} \tag{47}E[Ik​×Δln(a~it​/a~t​)]=0,E[Ik​×Δln(b~it​/b~t​)]=0,k∈{1,…,KI​}(47)

That is, the mean change in log fundamentals is zero in every distance cell: the systematic change in the gradient of economic activity relative to the pre-war CBD must be explained by the mechanisms of the model (commuting access and the two externalities) and not by systematic changes in fundamentals. The assumption is plausible because division stemmed from military considerations and reunification from the collapse of Communism. No moments are imposed on φ~i\tilde{\varphi}_iφ~​i​, because the density of development may itself respond to the shock. Two further moments use data for West Berlin during division. The commuting moment requires that the number of workers who commute less than 30 minutes is the same in the model and in the data:

E[ψHMj−∑i∈ℵjωj/eντij∑s=1Sωs/eντisHRi]=0(48)\mathbb{E}\left[\psi H_{Mj}-\sum_{i\in\aleph_j}\frac{\omega_j/e^{\nu\tau_{ij}}}{\sum_{s=1}^{S}\omega_s/e^{\nu\tau_{is}}}H_{Ri}\right]=0 \tag{48}E​ψHMj​−i∈ℵj​∑​∑s=1S​ωs​/eντis​ωj​/eντij​​HRi​​=0(48)

where ψ\psiψ is the fraction of workers commuting less than 30 minutes in the data and ℵj\aleph_jℵj​ is the set of residence blocks within 30 minutes of workplace jjj. The wage moment requires that the variance of log adjusted wages equals the variance of log wages across districts in the data, σln⁡wi2\sigma^2_{\ln w_i}σlnwi​2​:

E[(1/ε)2ln⁡(ωj)2−σln⁡wi2]=0(49)\mathbb{E}\left[(1/\varepsilon)^2\ln(\omega_j)^2-\sigma^2_{\ln w_i}\right]=0 \tag{49}E[(1/ε)2ln(ωj​)2−σlnwi​2​]=0(49)

Stacking the moment functions m(Xi,Λ)m(\mathbf{X}_i,\Lambda)m(Xi​,Λ) of the observed data Xi\mathbf{X}_iXi​, the efficient GMM estimator solves:

Λ^GMM=arg⁡min⁡(1N∑i=1Nm(Xi,Λ)′)W(1N∑i=1Nm(Xi,Λ))(50)\hat{\Lambda}_{GMM}=\arg\min\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}m(\mathbf{X}_i,\Lambda)'\right)\mathbb{W}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}m(\mathbf{X}_i,\Lambda)\right) \tag{50}Λ^GMM​=argmin(N1​i=1∑N​m(Xi​,Λ)′)W(N1​i=1∑N​m(Xi​,Λ))(50)

where W\mathbb{W}W is the efficient weighting matrix. The appendix describes the two-step procedure: a first step with the identity matrix, then the inverse of a heteroscedasticity and autocorrelation consistent estimate of the moment covariance in the spirit of Conley (1999) with a spatial lag of 0.5 kilometers. The model is estimated for division, for reunification, and pooling both.

Estimation Algorithm and Identification

Because the residuals have closed forms, the estimation always conditions on the same observed endogenous variables and never solves for a new equilibrium; this is what makes it robust to multiple equilibria and distinguishes it from simulated method of moments or indirect inference. The only costly step in evaluating the moments is the fixed point for transformed wages, with 15,937 blocks and about 254 million bilateral flows. Starting from a guess ω0\omega^0ω0, the algorithm computes predicted workplace employment H^M\hat{H}_MH^M​ from the matrix of commuting probabilities and observed residents, forms ω1=(HM/H^M)ω0\omega^1=(H_M/\hat{H}_M)\omega^0ω1=(HM​/H^M​)ω0, updates to ω2=0.5ω1+0.5ω0\omega^2=0.5\omega^1+0.5\omega^0ω2=0.5ω1+0.5ω0, and repeats; gross substitution guarantees rapid convergence to the unique solution. Blocks without workplace employment are assigned a zero wage. One evaluation takes about 30 seconds, and the outer minimization uses a pattern search in Matlab, with similar results from derivative-based and other global routines and from different starting values.

The identification argument follows the recursive structure.

  • ν\nuν: a higher ν\nuν makes commuting flows decline faster with travel time and raises the model's fraction of commutes below 30 minutes. No other parameter enters the commuting moment.

  • ε\varepsilonε: given ν\nuν, transformed wages are fixed, and a higher ε\varepsilonε lowers the dispersion of adjusted wages in the wage moment.

  • {λ,δ}\{\lambda,\delta\}{λ,δ} and {η,ρ}\{\eta,\rho\}{η,ρ}: although division is a single shock, the two sets are separately identified because A~i\tilde{A}_iA~i​ and B~i\tilde{B}_iB~i​ are recovered separately. The estimator is similar to an instrumental variables regression of changes in adjusted productivity on changes in Υi\Upsilon_iΥi​, and of changes in adjusted amenities on changes in Ωi\Omega_iΩi​, with the distance cells as instruments. The exclusion restrictions are that workplace employment density affects productivity but not amenities, and residence employment density affects amenities but not productivity. The elasticities control the size of the fall in externalities near the Wall, and the decay rates control how far it reaches into West Berlin; the parameters are chosen to make the mean change in log fundamentals as flat as possible across the distance cells.

The moment conditions need not identify the parameters uniquely in principle, since the objective is not globally concave. The appendix reports grid searches (20 values of ν\nuν; 20 values of ε\varepsilonε; 400 combinations each of {λ,δ}\{\lambda,\delta\}{λ,δ} and of {η,ρ}\{\eta,\rho\}{η,ρ}) that show a unique global minimum, and a Monte Carlo exercise on a hypothetical city recovers the true parameters.

Key Estimates

  • Pooled estimates (preferred): ν=0.0987\nu=0.0987ν=0.0987, ε=6.6941\varepsilon=6.6941ε=6.6941, λ=0.0710\lambda=0.0710λ=0.0710, δ=0.3617\delta=0.3617δ=0.3617, η=0.1553\eta=0.1553η=0.1553, ρ=0.7595\rho=0.7595ρ=0.7595, all significant at the 1 percent level, with κ=ν/ε=0.0148\kappa=\nu/\varepsilon=0.0148κ=ν/ε=0.0148.

  • Division: ν=0.0951\nu=0.0951ν=0.0951, ε=6.6190\varepsilon=6.6190ε=6.6190, λ=0.0793\lambda=0.0793λ=0.0793, δ=0.3585\delta=0.3585δ=0.3585, η=0.1548\eta=0.1548η=0.1548, ρ=0.9094\rho=0.9094ρ=0.9094. Reunification: ν=0.1011\nu=0.1011ν=0.1011, ε=6.7620\varepsilon=6.7620ε=6.7620, λ=0.0496\lambda=0.0496λ=0.0496, δ=0.9246\delta=0.9246δ=0.9246, η=0.0757\eta=0.0757η=0.0757, ρ=0.5531\rho=0.5531ρ=0.5531 (the last is not significant). Reunification is the smaller shock and gives less precise estimates.

  • Commuting: the estimates are close to those from the gravity equation (ν=0.07\nu=0.07ν=0.07, ε=6.83\varepsilon=6.83ε=6.83), and ε\varepsilonε is in the range of Frechet shape parameters estimated for international trade (3.60 to 12.86 in Eaton and Kortum 2002). After 10 minutes of travel, utility net of commuting costs is e−10κ=0.863e^{-10\kappa}=0.863e−10κ=0.863 of its initial level, and after 30 minutes 0.642. Long commutes are chosen only by workers with high draws for that pair.

  • Localization: production externalities e−δτe^{-\delta\tau}e−δτ fall to 0.696 after 1 minute, 0.485 after 2, 0.164 after 5 and 0.027 after 10 minutes of travel time; residential externalities e−ρτe^{-\rho\tau}e−ρτ fall to 0.468, 0.219, 0.022 and 0.001. Ten minutes correspond to about 0.83 kilometers on foot or about 4 kilometers by underground or suburban rail.

  • Comparison with the literature: λ=0.07\lambda=0.07λ=0.07 is toward the upper end of the 3 to 8 percent range surveyed by Rosenthal and Strange (2004) (the meta-analysis of Melo, Graham and Noland 2009 has a mean of 0.058) and below some quasi-experimental estimates (Greenstone, Hornbeck and Moretti 2010; Kline and Moretti 2014). Two points matter for the comparison. Zero profits link productivity to both wages and floor prices, so estimates based on wages alone understate productivity effects. And λ\lambdaλ is the effect of doubling employment density holding travel times constant, whereas a larger city also has longer travel times, which erode externalities at rate δ\deltaδ: production externalities from East Berlin raised the productivity of the median West Berlin block within 3.75 kilometers of the pre-war CBD by only 0.0121 log points in 1936, although spreading East Berlin's employment proportionally over West Berlin blocks would have raised it by 0.0710×ln⁡(1.7556)=0.04000.0710\times\ln(1.7556)=0.04000.0710×ln(1.7556)=0.0400. The rapid decay matches Arzaghi and Henderson (2008), who find little spillover beyond 500 meters among advertising agencies in Manhattan (about 9 minutes of travel time in the Berlin data, after which the estimated externality is about 4 percent), and the housing externalities of Rossi-Hansberg, Sarte and Owens (2010), which halve every 1,000 feet. Positive residential externalities are in line with endogenous amenities as in Glaeser, Kolko and Saiz (2001) and Diamond (2013).

Model Fit and Over-Identification Checks

In the estimation the model fits floor prices and employment exactly, because the residuals absorb everything, so fit must be judged on other grounds. (1) The commuting predictions for years and moments not used in estimation match the survey data, as described above. (2) The model-implied ratio of adjusted floor space to land area, L~i/Ki=φ~iKi−μ\tilde{L}_i/K_i=\tilde{\varphi}_iK_i^{-\mu}L~i​/Ki​=φ~​i​Ki−μ​, is strongly and approximately log-linearly related to a coarse measure of the floor space ratio in the data (coefficient 0.959 with standard error 0.018 and an R2R^2R2 of 0.36 in 2006). (3) Estimated residential fundamentals in 2006 are positively correlated with green areas, proximity to water and listed buildings and negatively with noise and wartime destruction, while production fundamentals are unrelated to noise. (4) The counterfactuals below show that the estimated externalities, rather than changes in fundamentals, account for the effects of division and reunification.

Counterfactuals

Counterfactual equilibria are computed with an iterative algorithm. Starting from observed floor prices, adjusted wages and commercial shares {Qi0,w~i0,θ~i0}\{\mathbb{Q}_i^0,\tilde{w}_i^0,\tilde{\theta}_i^0\}{Qi0​,w~i0​,θ~i0​}, commuting probabilities and hence HMi1H_{Mi}^1HMi1​ and HRi1H_{Ri}^1HRi1​ are computed with adjusted amenities and wages in place of their unadjusted counterparts, and new values follow from output, the labor share, expected residential income v~ˉi1=∑sπis∣i1w~s0\bar{\tilde{v}}_i^1=\sum_s\pi^1_{is|i}\tilde{w}_s^0v~ˉi1​=∑s​πis∣i1​w~s0​ and the two land market clearing conditions:

with θ~i1=1\tilde{\theta}_i^1=1θ~i1​=1 in ℑM\Im_MℑM​ and θ~i1=0\tilde{\theta}_i^1=0θ~i1​=0 in ℑR\Im_RℑR​. The guess is updated as a weighted average with weight 0<ς<10<\varsigma<10<ς<1 (in the appendix's notation for this step) until convergence:

Qi2=ςQi0+(1−ς)Qi1,w~i2=ςw~i0+(1−ς)w~i1,θ~i2=ςθ~i0+(1−ς)θ~i1(52)\mathbb{Q}_i^2=\varsigma\mathbb{Q}_i^0+(1-\varsigma)\mathbb{Q}_i^1,\qquad \tilde{w}_i^2=\varsigma\tilde{w}_i^0+(1-\varsigma)\tilde{w}_i^1,\qquad \tilde{\theta}_i^2=\varsigma\tilde{\theta}_i^0+(1-\varsigma)\tilde{\theta}_i^1 \tag{52}Qi2​=ςQi0​+(1−ς)Qi1​,w~i2​=ςw~i0​+(1−ς)w~i1​,θ~i2​=ςθ~i0​+(1−ς)θ~i1​(52)

With agglomeration forces the loop also updates Υi1\Upsilon_i^1Υi1​, A~i1=a~i(Υi1)λ\tilde{A}_i^1=\tilde{a}_i(\Upsilon_i^1)^{\lambda}A~i1​=a~i​(Υi1​)λ, Ωi1\Omega_i^1Ωi1​ and B~i1=b~i(Ωi1)η\tilde{B}_i^1=\tilde{b}_i(\Omega_i^1)^{\eta}B~i1​=b~i​(Ωi1​)η from the new employment vectors. Since the equilibrium may then not be unique, the equilibrium selection rule is to start from the observed equilibrium and thus find the counterfactual equilibrium closest to it. The aim is not to determine the unique effect of the shock but to see whether the estimated model can generate effects close to the observed ones. The reservation utility is chosen so that total population matches the data (West Berlin in 1986, Berlin in 2006). The counterfactual floor prices are then used in the reduced-form regression.

  • Division with estimated externalities (pooled estimates, fundamentals {a~i,b~i,φ~i}\{\tilde{a}_i,\tilde{b}_i,\tilde{\varphi}_i\}{a~i​,b~i​,φ~​i​} held at 1936 values): the first-cell coefficient is −0.836-0.836−0.836 against an observed −0.800-0.800−0.800, and the gradient declines to −0.349-0.349−0.349 in the sixth cell against an observed −0.291-0.291−0.291. The model with agglomeration forces accounts for the observed effect, whereas the model with exogenous characteristics delivers about half of the first-cell effect and no gradient.

  • Decomposition: without residential externalities (η=0\eta=0η=0) the first-cell coefficient is −0.613-0.613−0.613, and without production externalities (λ=0\lambda=0λ=0) it is −0.467-0.467−0.467; both externalities matter. Halving the decay rates {δ,ρ}\{\delta,\rho\}{δ,ρ} gives −0.821-0.821−0.821 in the first cell and larger effects in more distant cells (−0.430-0.430−0.430 in the sixth), so the effect reaches further into West Berlin.

  • Reunification (West Berlin fundamentals at 1986 values, East Berlin at 2006 values): the first-cell coefficient is 0.363 against an observed 0.398, and 0.392 with the division estimates. With 1936 fundamentals for East Berlin it would be 1.160: a recovery of East Berlin to its pre-war relative position would reorient West Berlin much further.

  • Transport technology: removing the automobile (2006 travel times based on public transport only, reservation utility held constant) raises the unweighted mean travel time from 51 to 70 minutes and the commuting-weighted mean from 32 to 38 minutes. Workers leave the city until floor prices have fallen enough: total employment falls by about 14 percent, output by about 12 percent and floor prices by 20 percent on average (29 percent in blocks with above-median increases in travel time, 11 percent in the others). Blocks become less specialized in workplace or residence activity, and with the new sorting the commuting-weighted travel time in the counterfactual equilibrium (30 minutes) is slightly below the actual one.

The supplement contains no formal extensions; it notes that the model can be extended to nontraded goods consumed at workplace and residence, to dependents who consume but do not work, to nonlabor income, and to land rents redistributed lump sum, and it abstracts from worker heterogeneity other than the idiosyncratic shock.

This is the primitive utility function of the model. Worker ooo who lives in block iii and works in block jjj consumes cijoc_{ijo}cijo​ units of the final good (the numeraire) and ℓijo\ell_{ijo}ℓijo​ units of residential floor space; β\betaβ is the expenditure share of the final good and 1−β1-\beta1−β that of floor space. The Cobb-Douglas aggregate is scaled by three terms: the amenity BiB_iBi​ common to all residents of iii, the idiosyncratic shock zijoz_{ijo}zijo​ specific to the worker and to the pair of residence and workplace, and the iceberg commuting cost dij=eκτij≥1d_{ij}=e^{\kappa\tau_{ij}}\ge1dij​=eκτij​≥1, which divides utility and grows exponentially in travel time τij\tau_{ij}τij​ at rate κ\kappaκ.

Dividing cijoc_{ijo}cijo​ by β\betaβ and ℓijo\ell_{ijo}ℓijo​ by 1−β1-\beta1−β is only a normalization: it makes the constants ββ(1−β)1−β\beta^{\beta}(1-\beta)^{1-\beta}ββ(1−β)1−β disappear from the indirect utility in equation (4). Because the worker is risk neutral, CijoC_{ijo}Cijo​ is both the consumption index and utility, so expected utility is simply the mean of the index.

The functional form buys two things. First, constant expenditure shares (equation (3)), so that the demand for floor space is linear in the wage. Second, BiB_iBi​, zijoz_{ijo}zijo​ and 1/dij1/d_{ij}1/dij​ enter multiplicatively, so indirect utility is proportional to the shock and inherits its Frechet distribution (equation (5)). The exponential form of dijd_{ij}dij​ implies that the log of utility falls linearly in travel time,

ln⁡Cijo=ln⁡Bi+ln⁡zijo−κτij+βln⁡cijoβ+(1−β)ln⁡ℓijo1−β,\ln C_{ijo}=\ln B_i+\ln z_{ijo}-\kappa\tau_{ij}+\beta\ln\frac{c_{ijo}}{\beta}+(1-\beta)\ln\frac{\ell_{ijo}}{1-\beta},lnCijo​=lnBi​+lnzijo​−κτij​+βlnβcijo​​+(1−β)ln1−βℓijo​​,

which is why the gravity equation (42) is semi-logarithmic in travel time. With the pooled estimate κ=0.0148\kappa=0.0148κ=0.0148, a commute of 30 minutes scales utility by e−30κ=0.642e^{-30\kappa}=0.642e−30κ=0.642.

This is the distributional assumption that makes the model tractable. Every worker draws one shock zijoz_{ijo}zijo​ for each of the S2S^2S2 pairs of residence block iii and workplace block jjj, independently across pairs and workers, from a Frechet (type II extreme value) distribution with cumulative distribution function FFF. The support is (0,∞)(0,\infty)(0,∞): F(z)→0F(z)\to0F(z)→0 as z→0z\to0z→0 and F(z)→1F(z)\to1F(z)→1 as z→∞z\to\inftyz→∞.

The product TiEjT_iE_jTi​Ej​ is the scale parameter. A larger TiT_iTi​ shifts the distribution of shocks for every pair with residence iii to the right, and a larger EjE_jEj​ does the same for every pair with workplace jjj; they capture average unobserved tastes for living in iii and working in jjj. The shape parameter ε\varepsilonε governs dispersion: the density is

f(z)=dF(z)dz=εTiEjz−(ε+1)e−TiEjz−ε,f(z)=\frac{dF(z)}{dz}=\varepsilon T_iE_jz^{-(\varepsilon+1)}e^{-T_iE_jz^{-\varepsilon}},f(z)=dzdF(z)​=εTi​Ej​z−(ε+1)e−Ti​Ej​z−ε,

and the mean, computed exactly as in equations (7) and (8), is

E[zijo]=Γ(ε−1ε)(TiEj)1/ε,\mathbb{E}[z_{ijo}]=\Gamma\left(\frac{\varepsilon-1}{\varepsilon}\right)(T_iE_j)^{1/\varepsilon},E[zijo​]=Γ(εε−1​)(Ti​Ej​)1/ε,

which is finite only if ε>1\varepsilon>1ε>1; this is the reason for that restriction. The standard deviation of ln⁡zijo\ln z_{ijo}lnzijo​ is π/(ε6)\pi/(\varepsilon\sqrt{6})π/(ε6​) (here π\piπ is the number 3.14...), so a larger ε\varepsilonε means workers are more alike, and their choices respond more strongly to wages, floor prices and commuting costs; ε\varepsilonε becomes the elasticity of commuting flows in equation (12).

What the Frechet form buys is closure under maximization: the maximum of independent Frechet variables with a common shape is again Frechet (equation (6)), which gives closed forms for expected utility (equation (8)) and for choice probabilities (equation (12)). What it rules out is correlation of shocks across pairs that share a residence or a workplace, and it imposes the independence of irrelevant alternatives visible in equation (12).

Combine three earlier results. Equation (8) gives the expected utility of moving to the city as E[u]=γΦ1/ε\mathbb{E}[u]=\gamma\Phi^{1/\varepsilon}E[u]=γΦ1/ε; equation (6) defines Φ=∑r∑sΦrs\Phi=\sum_r\sum_s\Phi_{rs}Φ=∑r​∑s​Φrs​; and equation (5) gives Φrs=TrEs(drsQr1−β)−ε(Brws)ε\Phi_{rs}=T_rE_s\left(d_{rs}Q_r^{1-\beta}\right)^{-\varepsilon}(B_rw_s)^{\varepsilon}Φrs​=Tr​Es​(drs​Qr1−β​)−ε(Br​ws​)ε. Workers are perfectly mobile between the city and the wider economy, where they obtain Uˉ\bar{U}Uˉ, and they are risk neutral and choose before observing the shocks. An equilibrium with a positive and finite city population therefore requires

γ[∑r=1S∑s=1STrEs(drsQr1−β)−ε(Brws)ε]1/ε=Uˉ.\gamma\left[\sum_{r=1}^{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}T_rE_s\left(d_{rs}Q_r^{1-\beta}\right)^{-\varepsilon}(B_rw_s)^{\varepsilon}\right]^{1/\varepsilon}=\bar{U}.γ[r=1∑S​s=1∑S​Tr​Es​(drs​Qr1−β​)−ε(Br​ws​)ε]1/ε=Uˉ.

Read as a labor supply function for block jjj, the right-hand side is continuous and strictly increasing in wjw_jwj​, with elasticity ε(1−πij∣i)\varepsilon(1-\pi_{ij|i})ε(1−πij∣i​) for each origin iii, and decreasing in the wages of competing workplaces. The income of a worker is the wage of the block where she works; the idiosyncratic shock zijoz_{ijo}zijo​ and the commuting cost dijd_{ij}dij​ affect utility but, in the interpretation adopted in the note, not the budget constraint cijo+Qiℓijo=wjc_{ijo}+Q_i\ell_{ijo}=w_jcijo​+Qi​ℓijo​=wj​ behind equation (3). For a resident of iii, income is therefore a discrete random variable that takes the value wjw_jwj​ when workplace jjj is chosen. This equation makes productivity endogenous. AjA_jAj​ is the productivity that firms in block jjj take as given in equation (19). It is the product of a production fundamental aja_jaj​, which is an exogenous feature of the location (for example access to water or the quality of the ground), and a spillover term Υjλ\Upsilon_j^{\lambda}Υjλ​. The production externality Υj\Upsilon_jΥj​ is a weighted sum over all blocks sss of workplace employment density HMs/KsH_{Ms}/K_sHMs​/Ks​ (workers per unit of land area), with weights e−δτjse^{-\delta\tau_{js}}e−δτjs​ that fall exponentially with the travel time τjs\tau_{js}τjs​ between jjj and sss.

Two parameters govern the externality. λ≥0\lambda\ge0λ≥0 is the elasticity of productivity with respect to the surrounding employment density: if employment doubles in every block, Υj\Upsilon_jΥj​ doubles and productivity rises by the factor 2λ2^{\lambda}2λ, which is 1.051.051.05 for the pooled estimate λ=0.071\lambda=0.071λ=0.071. δ≥0\delta\ge0δ≥0 is the rate of spatial decay per minute: the weight on a block τ\tauτ minutes away is

e−δτ=0.696, 0.164, 0.027for τ=1, 5, 10 minutes when δ=0.3617.e^{-\delta\tau}=0.696,\ 0.164,\ 0.027\qquad\text{for }\tau=1,\ 5,\ 10\ \text{minutes when }\delta=0.3617 .e−δτ=0.696, 0.164, 0.027for τ=1, 5, 10 minutes when δ=0.3617.

As δ→∞\delta\to\inftyδ→∞ only the own block counts, and with δ=0\delta=0δ=0 every block in the city has the same Υ\UpsilonΥ and the externality only shifts productivity uniformly. Density is measured per unit of land and not of floor space, so taller buildings raise the externality.

The multiplicative form means that ln⁡Aj=ln⁡aj+λln⁡Υj\ln A_j=\ln a_j+\lambda\ln\Upsilon_jlnAj​=lnaj​+λlnΥj​, which is what turns the fundamental into a residual that is linear in the parameters given δ\deltaδ (equation (45)). Firms ignore their own effect on Υ\UpsilonΥ, so this is an externality and the equilibrium is generally inefficient and possibly not unique. Division of the city is modeled as δ→∞\delta\to\inftyδ→∞ across the Wall, which removes East Berlin blocks from the sum. In the estimation the own block is left out of the sum to avoid a mechanical correlation.

This is the residential counterpart of equation (30). and residential spillovers are essentially confined to the immediate neighborhood.

This is the reduced-form difference-in-differences regression, estimated on blocks of West Berlin, separately for division (1936 to 1986) and reunification (1986 to 2006). The dependent variable Δln⁡Oi\Delta\ln O_iΔlnOi​ is the long difference in the log of an outcome of block iii: the floor price, workplace employment or residence employment. Differencing removes any time-invariant block characteristic. Iik\mathbb{I}_{ik}Iik​ equals one if block iii lies in the kkk-th distance cell from the pre-war CBD (six cells: the first for blocks less than 1.25 kilometers away, since the CBD lies east of the Wall, then intervals of 500 meters up to 3.75 kilometers), MiM_iMi​ are time-invariant controls whose effect on growth is allowed to be non-zero, and uiu_iui​ is the error. In this equation only, α\alphaα, βk\beta_kβk​ and γ\gammaγ are regression coefficients and not the model parameters with the same letters.

The constant α\alphaα is the mean log change in the omitted group, blocks more than 3.75 kilometers from the pre-war CBD, and βk\beta_kβk​ is the differential change of cell kkk relative to that group:

βk=E[Δln⁡Oi∣Iik=1,Mi]−E[Δln⁡Oi∣beyond 3.75 km,Mi].\beta_k=\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta\ln O_i\mid\mathbb{I}_{ik}=1,M_i\right]-\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta\ln O_i\mid\text{beyond 3.75 km},M_i\right].βk​=E[ΔlnOi​∣Iik​=1,Mi​]−E[ΔlnOi​∣beyond 3.75 km,Mi​].

The treatment is the loss (or recovery) of access to the pre-war CBD and East Berlin, whose intensity falls with distance; the cells estimate this gradient non-parametrically. The identifying assumption is that, absent division, blocks close to and far from the pre-war CBD would have had the same floor price and employment growth conditional on MiM_iMi​. It is supported by the absence of pre-trends and by coefficients near zero for distance to other parts of the Wall. A coefficient is converted to a percentage change by eβk−1e^{\beta_k}-1eβk​−1: for division β1=−0.800\beta_1=-0.800β1​=−0.800 gives e−0.8−1=−0.55e^{-0.8}-1=-0.55e−0.8−1=−0.55, a fall of 55 percent; for reunification β1=0.398\beta_1=0.398β1​=0.398 gives a rise of 49 percent.

The same specification is reused later with the recovered A~i\tilde{A}_iA~i​ and B~i\tilde{B}_iB~i​ and with counterfactual floor prices on the left-hand side, which makes the reduced form the yardstick for the structural model.

Take the log of the bilateral commuting probability, equation (12), with Φij\Phi_{ij}Φij​ from equation (5):

ln⁡πij=ln⁡Ti+ln⁡Ej−εln⁡dij−(1−β)εln⁡Qi+εln⁡Bi+εln⁡wj−ln⁡Φ.\ln\pi_{ij}=\ln T_i+\ln E_j-\varepsilon\ln d_{ij}-(1-\beta)\varepsilon\ln Q_i+\varepsilon\ln B_i+\varepsilon\ln w_j-\ln\Phi .lnπij​=lnTi​+lnEj​−εlndij​−(1−β)εlnQi​+εlnBi​+εlnwj​−lnΦ.

Insert the commuting cost dij=eκτijd_{ij}=e^{\kappa\tau_{ij}}dij​=eκτij​, so that εln⁡dij=εκτij=ντij\varepsilon\ln d_{ij}=\varepsilon\kappa\tau_{ij}=\nu\tau_{ij}εlndij​=εκτij​=ντij​, and group the remaining terms by the index on which they depend:

ln⁡πij=−ντij+[ln⁡Ti+εln⁡Bi−(1−β)εln⁡Qi]⏟ϑi+[ln⁡Ej+εln⁡wj]⏟ςj−ln⁡Φ.\ln\pi_{ij}=-\nu\tau_{ij}+\underbrace{\left[\ln T_i+\varepsilon\ln B_i-(1-\beta)\varepsilon\ln Q_i\right]}_{\vartheta_i}+\underbrace{\left[\ln E_j+\varepsilon\ln w_j\right]}_{\varsigma_j}-\ln\Phi .lnπij​=−ντij​+ϑi​[lnTi​+εlnBi​−(1−β)εlnQi​]​​+ςj​[lnEj​+εlnwj​]​​−lnΦ.

The first bracket varies only with the residence and the second only with the workplace, so they are captured by residence and workplace fixed effects; ln⁡Φ\ln\PhilnΦ is a constant common to all pairs and is absorbed by either set of fixed effects. Adding a stochastic error eije_{ij}eij​ gives the estimating equation

ln⁡πij=−ντij+ϑi+ςj+eij.\ln\pi_{ij}=-\nu\tau_{ij}+\vartheta_i+\varsigma_j+e_{ij}.lnπij​=−ντij​+ϑi​+ςj​+eij​.

The equation is linear in travel time and not in its log because the commuting cost is exponential, so ν\nuν is a semi-elasticity: one more minute lowers the flow by 1−e−ν1-e^{-\nu}1−e−ν, about 7 percent for ν=0.07\nu=0.07ν=0.07. The residual depends on four parameters: ν\nuν (through WitW_{it}Wit​), ε\varepsilonε, η\etaη and ρ\rhoρ (through Ωit\Omega_{it}Ωit​). The equation states the accounting behind the amenity estimates. After division, blocks near the Wall lost residents and their floor prices fell, which lowers the first two terms. Part of this is explained by the loss of access to jobs in East Berlin, a fall in WitW_{it}Wit​, which enters with a minus sign and so raises the residual back toward zero. Whatever remains must be attributed either to lower residential externalities, the term in η\etaη, or to a deterioration of fundamentals, and the moment conditions of equation (47) rule out the latter on average within distance cells. Dividing by geometric means removes the changes in Uˉt\bar{U}_tUˉt​ and in total population between years.

These are the main moment conditions of the structural estimation. Ik\mathbb{I}_kIk​ is an indicator that block iii belongs to the kkk-th of KI=50K_{\mathbb{I}}=50KI​=50 cells defined by percentiles of distance to the pre-war CBD, and the two terms multiplied by it are the double-differenced structural residuals of equations (45) and (46). Since the indicators are mutually exclusive, the conditions are equivalent to

E[Δln⁡(a~it/a~‾t)∣Ik=1]=0,E[Δln⁡(b~it/b~‾t)∣Ik=1]=0for every k,\mathbb{E}\left[\Delta\ln\left(\tilde{a}_{it}/\overline{\tilde{a}}_t\right)\mid\mathbb{I}_k=1\right]=0,\qquad \mathbb{E}\left[\Delta\ln\left(\tilde{b}_{it}/\overline{\tilde{b}}_t\right)\mid\mathbb{I}_k=1\right]=0\qquad\text{for every } k,E[Δln(a~it​/a~t​)∣Ik​=1]=0,E[Δln(b~it​/b~t​)∣Ik​=1]=0for every k,

that is, the average change in relative log fundamentals is the same (zero) at every distance from the pre-war CBD. Individual blocks may have any shock; only a systematic relation between shocks to fundamentals and distance to the pre-war CBD is ruled out.

The logic is that of instrumental variables. Division removed the employment and residents of East Berlin from the sums Υit\Upsilon_{it}Υit​ and Ωit\Omega_{it}Ωit​, and the size of this loss is a function of distance to the pre-war CBD. The distance cells therefore predict the change in the externalities, and they are assumed to be excluded from the change in fundamentals, which is credible because the border followed military considerations and pre-war district boundaries. The parameters λ\lambdaλ and η\etaη are identified by how much productivity and amenities fell where the externality fell most, and δ\deltaδ and ρ\rhoρ by how fast this effect fades with distance from the Wall: the estimates make the mean residuals as flat as possible across the cells.

There are 2KI=1002K_{\mathbb{I}}=1002KI​=100 such moments. Because the residuals are measured relative to geometric means, their overall mean is zero by construction when the same sample is used, so one moment in each set is implied by the others. Together with the moments of equations (48) and (49) they over-identify the six parameters. No analogous moment is imposed on the density of development, which may respond to the shock.

This moment pins down the commuting semi-elasticity ν\nuν using commuting data for West Berlin during division. Identification is transparent. The transformed wages ωj\omega_jωj​ are themselves solved from equation (36) for each trial value of ν\nuν, so the moment is a function of ν\nuν and data only; neither ε\varepsilonε nor the agglomeration parameters enter. A higher ν\nuν makes flows decline faster with travel time, which raises the model's share of commutes below 30 minutes monotonically, so one moment determines one parameter. This plays the role that the gravity regression (42) plays in the calibration, and gives ν\nuν of about 0.10 against 0.07 from the regression on 2008 district data. The threshold of 30 minutes is a choice; the model's fit to the whole distribution of commuting times serves as a check.

This moment identifies the Frechet shape parameter ε\varepsilonε. Given ν\nuν, the transformed wages ωj\omega_jωj​ are known from equation (36), and adjusted wages are w~j=ωj1/ε\tilde{w}_j=\omega_j^{1/\varepsilon}w~j​=ωj1/ε​, so

The moment therefore equates the mean squared log adjusted wage in the model to the variance of log wages in the data.

A mean square is not in general a variance:

E[(ln⁡w~j)2]=Var⁡(ln⁡w~j)+(E[ln⁡w~j])2.\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\ln\tilde{w}_j\right)^{2}\right]=\operatorname{Var}\left(\ln\tilde{w}_j\right)+\left(\mathbb{E}\left[\ln\tilde{w}_j\right]\right)^{2}.E[(lnw~j​)2]=Var(lnw~j​)+(E[lnw~j​])2.

Solving the moment for the parameter gives

ε^=σln⁡ωjσln⁡wi,\hat{\varepsilon}=\frac{\sigma_{\ln\omega_j}}{\sigma_{\ln w_i}},ε^=σlnwi​​σlnωj​​​,

the ratio of the standard deviation of log transformed wages to that of log wages in the data. The intuition: a given pattern of commuting flows can be produced by small wage differences with a high elasticity or by large wage differences with a low elasticity, and the observed wage dispersion selects between them. Two caveats in interpreting it are that the data are for districts while the model moment is across blocks, and that the model object is the adjusted wage, which includes the workplace draw Ej1/εE_j^{1/\varepsilon}Ej1/ε​. The result is ε\varepsilonε of about 6.7 to 6.8.

This is the generalized method of moments estimator of the parameter vector Λ={ν,ε,λ,δ,η,ρ}\Lambda=\{\nu,\varepsilon,\lambda,\delta,\eta,\rho\}Λ={ν,ε,λ,δ,η,ρ}. The vector m(Xi,Λ)m(\mathbf{X}_i,\Lambda)m(Xi​,Λ) stacks, for observation (block) iii with data Xi\mathbf{X}_iXi​, the moment functions whose expectations are zero at the true parameters: the 2KI2K_{\mathbb{I}}2KI​ products of distance cell indicators and structural residuals from equation (47), the commuting moment (48) and the wage moment (49). The term in parentheses is the vector of sample means of the moments over the NNN blocks, and W\mathbb{W}W is a symmetric positive definite weighting matrix. The objective is a quadratic form, a weighted squared distance of the sample moments from zero:

J(Λ)=mˉ(Λ)′ W mˉ(Λ),mˉ(Λ)=1N∑i=1Nm(Xi,Λ).J(\Lambda)=\bar{m}(\Lambda)'\,\mathbb{W}\,\bar{m}(\Lambda),\qquad \bar{m}(\Lambda)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}m(\mathbf{X}_i,\Lambda).J(Λ)=mˉ(Λ)′Wmˉ(Λ),mˉ(Λ)=N1​i=1∑N​m(Xi​,Λ).

There are 102 moments and 6 parameters, so the sample moments cannot all be set to zero and the weighting matrix decides how the deviations are traded off. The efficient choice is the inverse of the covariance matrix of the moments, which gives less weight to noisy moments. It is implemented in two steps: first minimize with the identity matrix to obtain a consistent estimate, then estimate the covariance matrix of the moments at that estimate, allowing for heteroscedasticity and for spatial correlation between blocks within 0.5 kilometers in the manner of Conley (1999), and minimize again with its inverse. Standard errors come from the usual sandwich formula with the same covariance estimate.

Two features are specific to this application. First, m(⋅)m(\cdot)m(⋅) is available in closed form given the data, apart from the fixed point for transformed wages in equation (36), so evaluating the objective never requires solving for an equilibrium of the model; the estimator is therefore valid even if the model has multiple equilibria. Second, the problem has a recursive structure: ν\nuν is determined by the commuting moment, ε\varepsilonε by the wage moment given ν\nuν, and the pairs {λ,δ}\{\lambda,\delta\}{λ,δ} and {η,ρ}\{\eta,\rho\}{η,ρ} by the two sets of residual moments. The objective is not globally concave, so the paper checks the minimum with grid searches and different starting values.

A point to flag: for mixed blocks (ℑS\Im_SℑS​) the two price formulas, equations (S.78) and (S.79) of the supplement, both define Qi1\mathbb{Q}_i^1Qi1​, and for an arbitrary guess θ~i0\tilde{\theta}_i^0θ~i0​ they give different numbers; neither the supplement nor the note says which one is used. They coincide only at a fixed point, where equating them gives

which is the no-arbitrage condition: the share adjusts until both uses pay the same observed price. Note also that if the commercial formula were used for Qi1\mathbb{Q}_i^1Qi1​ in the last line, it would return θ~i1=θ~i0\tilde{\theta}_i^1=\tilde{\theta}_i^0θ~i1​=θ~i0​ identically, so for the share to be updated the price there must come from the residential side or from a combination such as the price that clears the total floor space market, Qi1=[(1−α)Yi1+(1−β)v~ˉi1HRi1]/(φ~iKi1−μ)\mathbb{Q}_i^1=[(1-\alpha)Y_i^1+(1-\beta)\bar{\tilde{v}}_i^1H_{Ri}^1]/(\tilde{\varphi}_iK_i^{1-\mu})Qi1​=[(1−α)Yi1​+(1−β)v~ˉi1​HRi1​]/(φ~​i​Ki1−μ​). All these variants have the same fixed points, so the counterfactual equilibrium is not affected.

This is the updating step of the counterfactual algorithm. Superscript 0 denotes the current guess of observed floor prices, adjusted wages and commercial shares, superscript 1 the values implied by the equilibrium conditions in equation (51) given that guess, and superscript 2 the guess for the next iteration. The weight ς∈(0,1)\varsigma\in(0,1)ς∈(0,1) is a damping parameter; it is the supplement's notation for this step and is unrelated to the workplace fixed effect ςj\varsigma_jςj​ of equation (42).

Writing xxx for any of the three variables, the update can be rearranged as

xi2=ςxi0+(1−ς)xi1=xi0+(1−ς)(xi1−xi0),x_i^2=\varsigma x_i^0+(1-\varsigma)x_i^1=x_i^0+(1-\varsigma)\left(x_i^1-x_i^0\right),xi2​=ςxi0​+(1−ς)xi1​=xi0​+(1−ς)(xi1​−xi0​),

so the guess moves a fraction 1−ς1-\varsigma1−ς of the way toward the implied value. The guess stops changing, xi2=xi0x_i^2=x_i^0xi2​=xi0​, if and only if xi1=xi0x_i^1=x_i^0xi1​=xi0​, that is, exactly when the guess reproduces itself through equation (51) and is therefore an equilibrium. Damping does not change the set of fixed points; it only affects the path. Jumping directly to the implied values (ς=0\varsigma=0ς=0) tends to overshoot and oscillate, because a high price guess in a block implies low employment and hence a low implied price; a larger ς\varsigmaς gives smaller, more stable steps at the cost of more iterations. A convex combination also keeps prices and wages positive and the commercial share between zero and one.

With exogenous location characteristics the equilibrium is unique (Proposition 1), so the starting point is irrelevant. With agglomeration forces the loop also recomputes the externalities of equations (30) and (31) from the new employment vectors, and several equilibria may exist. Starting from the observed equilibrium and taking damped steps is then the paper's equilibrium selection rule: the algorithm converges to a counterfactual equilibrium near the observed one. The same damped iteration, with weight 0.5, is used for transformed wages in the estimation.
